newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian rebels get ready for fight in south.
newsitem.headline: Albanian rebels get ready for fight in south.

text.p: Heavily armed Albanian rebels in this picturesque port fortified hilltop defences on Thursday but delayed sending their pro-government prisoners to a "people's court" in the town square.
Rebels who took control of Sarande during anti-government riots at the weekend dug in on hilltops and moved seized tanks into position at the eastern entrance to the town.
Insurgent checkpoints materialised and increasingly well-built barricades raised to defend Sarande against any attempt to crush the uprising by regular army troops.
"This is a popular uprising and won't stop until (President Sali) Berisha resigns," a former army officer called Davar told an evening rally of thousands in the main square.

He also said that youngsters under 16 would be disarmed in an attempt to restore order. Even pre-teen children have wandered through the town firing off bursts from assault rifles and struggled to reload ammunition clips.
Thousands of locals joined the uprising against Berisha, seizing an array of weapons from state arsenals during weekend rioting.
Sarande sits in the far southwestern corner of the small Balkan country, just across from the Greek island of Corfu and just north of the Greek border.
For five days locals have run riot, firing new Khalashnikov assault rifles in the air, driving a seized tank around town and sporting headscarves and ghoulish masks to hide their faces.

But former army officers, siding with the rebels, organised hundreds of gunmen into units, set up well-fortified defensive positions and established radio links with rebel strongholds in the nearby hills.

"We're telling everyone to uncover their faces. We're not criminals. We're freedom fighters who are fighting for everyone in Sarande," a group leader at the main hilltop barricade at the entrance to Sarande told Reuters.
Heavy machine-guns and anti-aircraft artillery were being placed around the position and camouflage was used to cover weapons for the first time.
Rebel groups were also moving into the hill country to the north of Sarande, where the first clash took place with about 60 army regulars on Wednesday.
In Sarande, several people accused of being police agents or sympathisers were held by rebels, who said they would face a "people's court" in the town square on Thursday.
But rebel leaders said the "trials" had been postponed. They gave no reason.

The rebels tied a police suspect to a telephone pole and kicked him in the face on Wednesday. He was dragged before an enraged mob in the square where he "confessed" over a public address system. His fate is unknown.
Sarande was mostly quiet on Thursday, unlike previous days this week when bursts of automatic rifle fire have filled the air as boys and men alike tried out their new weapons.
There was less spontaneous gunfire on Thursday and most people were busy preparing for a possible assault.
A tank was seized on Wednesday and paraded around town with a pack of gunmen aboard. But on Thursday it was set up behind a defensive position along with other captured tanks.
A main bridge about 20 km (12 miles) east of Sarande was bombed on Wednesday, limiting access to the coastal town from army barracks to the north or the Greek border to the south.
